template_name: Architectural Threshold Properties and Episodic Boundary Encoding (Doorway Effect)

mechanism_chain.process: Occupant approaches architectural threshold (doorway, archway, corridor transition, scale change). Sensory and motoric cues signal an impending environmental boundary.
mechanism_chain.substrate: Visual boundary detection (parahippocampal cortex); proprioceptive transition signals (vestibular, somatosensory)

data.finding: Passing through doorways produces memory decrements for recently considered objects/goals
Parahippocampal cortex responds to spatial scene boundaries; may detect environmental transitions

justification.backing: Radvansky's doorway effect demonstrates that architectural thresholds have cognitive consequences. The boundary is detected via visual scene processing (PPA) and proprioceptive cues (vestibular, motor) that signal transition between spatial contexts.
justification.qualifier: The doorway effect is robust; the specific neural mechanisms of boundary detection in architectural (vs. laboratory) settings are inferred.
justification.rebuttal: Would fail if doorway effects are due to distraction or attention shifts rather than true boundary encoding; but VR studies control for this and still show effects.

mechanism_chain.process: Boundary detection triggers event model updating: the current event model (maintained in working memory) is closed and stored as a completed episodic unit. A new event model is opened.
mechanism_chain.substrate: Prefrontal event model maintenance → hippocampal episodic encoding of completed event
mechanism_chain.source: Radvansky et al. (2011); Zacks et al. (2007)

data.finding: Event segmentation theory: ongoing experience is segmented into discrete events at boundaries; boundaries trigger updating of working memory event model
Prefrontal cortex maintains event models; hippocampus encodes completed events at boundaries

justification.backing: Zacks' event segmentation theory provides the framework for understanding how boundaries affect cognition. Crossing a boundary closes the current event model and opens a new one, with the closed model transferred from working memory to episodic storage.
justification.qualifier: Event segmentation is established; the specific mapping from architectural thresholds to event model updating is demonstrated for doorways but less tested for other threshold types.
justification.rebuttal: Would fail if event segmentation is purely cognitive (goal-driven) rather than environmentally triggered; but evidence shows physical boundaries drive segmentation even without task demands.

mechanism_chain.process: Information from the closed event model becomes less accessible (the doorway effect): recently active representations from the prior room are now stored in episodic memory and must be retrieved rather than simply maintained in working memory
mechanism_chain.substrate: Working memory → episodic memory transition; retrieval demand increases

data.finding: Memory for objects/goals held during room transition is impaired relative to same-distance movement within room
Effect occurs in VR, ruling out physical movement artifacts; boundary per se produces the memory shift

justification.backing: The doorway effect demonstrates that information maintained in working memory during one event becomes less accessible after a boundary is crossed. The information is not lost — it is transferred to episodic memory where retrieval is required.
justification.qualifier: The effect is robust but modest in size; working memory is not completely cleared at boundaries, just shifted.
justification.rebuttal: Would fail if the effect is due to distraction at doorways rather than true event model updating; but VR studies without physical doorways replicate the effect.

mechanism_chain.process: The boundary moment itself is encoded as a distinctive episodic marker — a temporal landmark that organizes the ongoing stream of experience into discrete episodes. Stronger boundaries produce more distinctive temporal landmarks.
mechanism_chain.substrate: Hippocampal time cell sequences reset at event boundaries (DuBrow & Davachi, 2013)

data.finding: Event boundaries produce discontinuities in temporal context representation; boundaries are remembered as temporal landmarks
Items at event boundaries are better remembered than mid-event items; boundary encoding is privileged

justification.backing: Event boundaries serve a double function: they segment experience into episodes AND they create memorable landmarks. The boundary moment itself is encoded more strongly than routine within-event experiences.
justification.qualifier: The temporal landmark effect is demonstrated for experimental boundaries; the translation to architectural thresholds of varying strength involves capacity assumptions.
justification.rebuttal: Would fail if architectural threshold strength does not modulate boundary encoding strength; the dose-response for threshold properties is predicted but not directly tested.

architectural_threshold.interpretation: Abrupt transitions (door frame, wall-to-wall) produce stronger episodic boundaries than gradual transitions (open archway, gradual ceiling slope). The abruptness modulates the rate of context change in TCM.

spatial_configuration.interpretation: The magnitude of change in spatial properties across the threshold: room size, ceiling height, lighting level, material palette. Larger contrasts are predicted to produce stronger episodic boundaries.
spatial_configuration.note: Predicted by TCM (Howard) and PE encoding (Davachi); not empirically tested parametrically

spatial_enclosure_ratio.interpretation: Any change in enclosure (from open to enclosed, from low to high ceiling, from narrow to wide) triggers some boundary encoding. The magnitude of enclosure change is predicted to modulate boundary strength, but this is untested.

dose_response_function.interpretation: TCM and PE encoding predict that boundary strength scales monotonically with spatial contrast ratio. This is a THEORETICAL_DEFAULT prediction: the binary effect (boundary present/absent) is well-established, but the dose-response has not been tested.

age_group.effect: The doorway effect is preserved or possibly larger in older adults (Radvansky et al., 2011). Older adults may be more susceptible to event model updating, making threshold design more impactful for this population.

cognitive_load.effect: Under high cognitive load, the doorway effect is amplified: more information is lost at boundaries because working memory capacity is already near limit when the event model update occurs

IC2_AX4_interaction.IC2_body_budget: Episodic boundary encoding may be modulated by body budget state: under allostatic deficit, occupants are less attentive to environmental transitions and may produce weaker event model updating. Alternatively, high arousal may amplify boundary detection (threat monitoring enhances environmental change detection). Direction is uncertain; confidence 0.30.
IC2_AX4_interaction.AX4_perceived_control: Thresholds that restrict perceived control (locked doors, narrow passages, forced single-file transitions) produce stronger episodic boundaries than thresholds that preserve control (open archways, wide passages). The control dimension adds to the spatial contrast effect. Conversely, thresholds that INCREASE perceived control (entering your own office from a shared corridor) may produce a positive episodic boundary — segmentation with relief rather than segmentation with anxiety.

architectural_threshold.interpretation: Change in acoustic, olfactory, or thermal conditions across the threshold. Multi-sensory discontinuity strengthens boundary encoding beyond visual-spatial contrast alone.
